topic: I want to add a cover crop this fall but I've never done it before. Where do I even start?

transcript.text: I’m basically at the same point. I’ve got about three-quarters of an acre in central Ohio, mostly raised beds of tomatoes, squash, and leaf greens, and I’m working with a spader and wheel hoe rather than a tiller. My first goal is keeping the soil covered over winter and suppressing weeds, but I’m worried about picking something that’ll be a nightmare to kill in spring. If you were starting from zero, what fall cover crop mix would you actually recommend for a small operation like mine?

**Quick‑Start Fall Cover‑Crop Mix for ¾ acre of raised beds in central Ohio** | Component | Why it’s useful | Seed rate (per acre) | Seed for 0.75 acre | |-----------|----------------|----------------------|-------------------| | **Winter (cereal) rye *Secale cerale*** | Fast‑growing, tolerates cold, gives a dense, weed‑suppressing mulch; roots stay alive over winter and add organic matter. | 70 lb (≈ 30 kg) | **≈ 52 lb / 23 kg** | | **Hairy vetch *Vicia villosa*** | Nitrogen‑fixing legume; adds N for your spring tomatoes, squash & greens; climbs over rye for a thick canopy. | 10 lb (≈ 4.5 kg) | **≈ 7.5 lb / 3.4 kg** | | **Crimson (or “red”) clover *Trifolium crimson*** | Additional N, attractive to pollinators, quick to establish, easy to terminate. | 5 lb (≈ 2.3 kg) | **≈ 3.8 lb / 1.7 kg** | | (Optional) **Radish “tillage‑breaker” *Raphanus sativus* (Daikon)** | Grows fast, its taproot cracks compact soil; dies back in winter leaving a channel for water. | 2 lb (≈ 0.9 kg) | **≈ 1.5 lb / 0.7 kg** | ### How to Plant 1. **Timing** – Aim for the **first week of October** (once you’ve finished harvesting tomatoes/squash). That gives 6‑8 weeks of growth before the first hard freeze. 2. **Seed‑mix preparation** – Blend the four components in a bucket so the percentages stay consistent. 3. **Broadcast** – Spread the mix evenly over the beds (a ¼‑inch‑deep layer of seed). With a wheel hoe you can gently rake the seed in about ½ inch of soil; no deep tilling needed. 4. **Moisture** – Water lightly after seeding and keep the soil moist for the first 7‑10 days until seedlings are established (≈ 2‑3 inches of soil moisture). ### What to Expect Over Winter - **Rye** will stay green and form a thick mat. In the coldest parts of your beds it may die back (which is fine – it still leaves a good mulch). - **Vetch and clover** will mostly flower early fall, then go dormant. Their roots keep feeding the soil and fixing nitrogen. - **Radish** will bolt and die back by mid‑winter, leaving a looser soil structure. ### Spring Termination (before you plant tomatoes again) | Method | When to do it | Steps | |--------|---------------|-------| | **Mow + crimp** (preferred for minimal disturbance) | When the rye is about 6‑8 in tall and vetch/clover are just starting to green up (late Feb‑early Mar) | 1️⃣ Mow the whole bed to ~2‑3 in.
2️⃣ Pass a garden roller or a heavy flail mower over the cut material to “crimp” the stems (breaks seed production).
3️⃣ Let the crimped mulch sit 1‑2 weeks; it will suppress weeds and release nitrogen as it decomposes. | | **Sharp cut & side‑dressed compost** (if you want a quick clear‑bed) | Same timing as above | 1️⃣ Cut with a scythe or string trimmer.
2️⃣ Rake the cut material into a thin layer or pull it off with a sheet mulching tarp.
3️⃣ Lightly work a thin (¼‑½‑in) layer of compost into the top 1 in of soil before planting. | > **Why this mix works for a “night‑mare‑free” spring** > • **Rye** is the easiest to kill – a single mowing + crimp or a shallow till after the first hard freeze usually does it. > • **Vetch & clover** are low‑profile legumes; when you mow “green‑up” in early spring they’re already thin and die back quickly, adding N without creating a thick, hard‑to‑remove stand. > • **Radish** is already dead by the time you start planting, leaving no extra biomass to manage. ### Practical Tips for a ¾‑acre (≈ 32,000 sq ft) Raised‑Bed System 1. **Buy seed in small packets** – Most seed companies sell 1‑lb packets of rye, vetch, or clover. For 0.75 acre you’ll need roughly ½‑lb of each legume and ~½‑lb of clover, plus ~½‑lb of radish if you use it. 2. **Check seed purity** – Choose “no‑hard‑seed” rye (e.g., “Winter Rye – No‑Weed” from Johnny’s or High Mowing) to avoid weed carry‑over. 3. **Avoid herbicide residues** – If you used any pre‑plant herbicide earlier in the season, wait the label‑specified pre‑harvest interval (usually 30‑45 days) before seeding the cover crop. 4. **Record dates** – Write down seeding date, last frost, and termination date. That makes it easy to fine‑tune rates next year. --- **Bottom line:** a simple three‑species blend—≈ 70 % winter rye, 25 % hairy vetch, 5 % crimson clover (plus a pinch of radish if you like) – seeded in early October, mowed/crimped in early spring, gives you a living mulch, nitrogen boost, and a bed that’s ready for tomatoes, squash, or greens without a dreaded “turn‑the‑soil‑into‑a‑weed‑seed‑bank” problem. *Let me know if you have any constraints (organic‑only seed sources, budget limits, or a preference for a no‑mow termination), and I can tweak the mix or suggest specific seed suppliers in Ohio.*

Okay, this is really helpful, but I'm already stuck on a couple of things. First — you keep saying mow and crimp, but I don't *have* a mower. I'm talking hand tools: a spader, a wheel hoe, maybe a string trimmer if I'm feeling ambitious. I'm not renting a flail mower for ¾ acre of raised beds. So how does someone like me actually terminate that rye in the spring without it just bouncing back and taking over?

And second, the seed quantities in that table versus the "practical tips" section at the bottom don't really line up for me. Are we talking fifty-something pounds of rye, or half a pound? Because if it's the former, I don't know where I'm buying that in a quantity I can actually handle and spread by hand into individual raised beds.

### 1. Terminating a winter‑rye / legume mix with **hand tools only** You don’t need a powered mower or a flail mower. The goal is to **cut the canopy, kill the remaining shoots, and either leave a mulch or turn the dead plant material into the soil**. Below are three low‑tech options that work well on a ¾‑acre (≈ 32 000 sq ft) set of raised beds. | Method | Tools you already have | How‑to do it (step‑by‑step) | Pros / Cons | |--------|-----------------------|------------------------------|-------------| | **A. Scythe or manual sickle cut + “step‑crimp”** | Scythe, sickle, or a sturdy **string‑trimmer** (set to a low‑cut “weed‑whacker” head) | 1. **Cut** the rye when it’s 6‑8 in tall (late Feb‑early Mar, just before the soil thaws).
2. Let the cut stalks dry for **1–2 weeks** (they’ll turn brown and become brittle).
3. Walk the beds **heel‑to‑toe** or use a **garden roller** (or a heavy board you push) to crush the dried stems – this is the “crimp.”
4. **Leave the crushed mat** on the surface; it will suppress weeds and release N as it decomposes. | Very cheap; minimal soil disturbance (good for soil microbes).
Needs a bit of muscle and a short waiting period for the stems to dry. | | **B. “Cut‑and‑bury” with a wheel hoe or spade** | Wheel hoe, spade, (optional) hand fork | 1. Use the **wheel hoe** to **slice** across the bed (think of mowing with a blade). A single pass at a shallow depth (≈ ½ in) will cut most of the rye.
2. **Walk the hoe back and forth** a second time, this time **tilting the wheel** so the blade cuts a little deeper (≈ 1‑1½ in) and throws the cut material sideways.
3. With the **spade** or a garden fork, **turn the cut residue** into the top 2‑3 in of soil. Work in ~3‑ft strips so you don’t have to lift the whole bed at once.
4. Water lightly and let the material decompose over the next 2‑3 weeks before you plant. | Gives you a ready‑made “green manuring” layer (extra organic matter).
More labor than crimping, but you already have the tools. | | **C. Sheet‑mulch “smother” (no cutting)** | Cardboard or several layers of newspaper, straw/pine mulch, wheel hoe | 1. **Mow or trim** the rye just enough to make the stand uniform (use the trimmer set low).
2. Lay **wet cardboard** (or 4‑6 sheets of newspaper) over the whole bed, overlapping edges.
3. Cover the cardboard with a **2‑in layer of straw or pine mulch** (you can use the shredded rye itself).
4. Keep the mulch in place for **4‑6 weeks**; the rye will die underneath and decompose into the mulch.
5. When you’re ready to plant, simply **pull the mulch aside** and you have a clean, weed‑free seedbed. | No cutting required; perfect if you’re short on time or want a “set‑and‑forget” approach.
Uses up extra organic material you may already have. | **Tip:** If you have a **hand‑crimper** (a garden roller with a toothed drum), you can use that after cutting—just push it over the dead stalks. They’re inexpensive (< $30 on Amazon) and store flat. --- ### 2. How much seed do you really need? (Clarifying the numbers) The rates in the table are **per full acre**. Since you have **0.75 acre** (≈ ¾ of an acre), you multiply each per‑acre amount by **0.75**. The resulting **total weight** is what you actually need to buy. | Crop | Recommended rate **per acre** | **0.75‑acre amount** | Approx. number of commercial packets (typical pack sizes) | |------|-------------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------| | **Winter rye** | 70 lb / acre (≈ 30 kg) | **≈ 52 lb (≈ 23 kg)** | 1 × 20‑lb bag + 1 × 15‑lb bag (or 3 × 20‑lb bags and keep the spare) | | **Hairy vetch** | 10 lb / acre (≈ 4.5 kg) | **≈ 7.5 lb (≈ 3.4 kg)** | 1 × 5‑lb bag + 1 × 2‑lb bag (or 2 × 5‑lb bags) | | **Crimson clover** | 5 lb / acre (≈ 2.3 kg) | **≈ 3.8 lb (≈ 1.7 kg)** | 1 × 4‑lb bag (most suppliers sell 4‑lb packets) | | **Daikon radish (optional)** | 2 lb / acre (≈ 0.9 kg) | **≈ 1.5 lb (≈ 0.7 kg)** | 1 × 1‑lb packet (or 1 × 2‑lb packet) | **Bottom line:** You’re looking at **≈ 65 lb (≈ 30 kg) of seed total**. That’s a handful of bags you can carry and broadcast by hand. --- ### 3. Where to buy the right‑size quantities (Ohio‑friendly) | Supplier | What they carry (small‑packet options) | Typical price (2024) | How to order | |----------|----------------------------------------|----------------------|--------------| | **Johnny’s Selected Seeds** (online, ships to Ohio) | Winter rye (20‑lb bag), Hairy vetch (5‑lb), Crimson clover (4‑lb), Daikon radish (1‑lb) | $12‑$18 per bag (rye a bit pricier) | Online shop – you can buy exactly the bag sizes shown above. | | **High Mowing Seeds** – “Organic” line | Same packet sizes, plus “No‑hard‑seed” rye (20‑lb) | $14‑$20 per bag | Online; they offer a “small‑farm” bundle (rye + vetch + clover) at a modest discount. | | **Local co‑ops / Ohio Agri‑Supply** (e.g., **Frostburg Farm Supply**, **Earl’s Seed & Feed**) | Often carry 5‑lb rye and 2‑lb vetch packets; you can combine a few. | $8‑$12 per small bag | Call ahead; many will let you buy the exact number of bags you need. | | **Farmers’ Market / Community Seed Swap** | Occasionally someone sells bulk bin seed at 5‑lb increments. | Variable (often cheaper) | Bring a reusable sack and ask for “winter rye, vetch, crimson clover.” | **Tip:** If you can’t find a 20‑lb rye bag, you can purchase several 5‑lb bags (e.g., 10 × 5‑lb = 50 lb) and mix them in a bucket to get your 52‑lb total. The important thing is a **clean, certified weed‑free seed** – avoid “field‑treated” or “no‑hard‑seed” labels unless you specifically want those traits. --- ### 4. Hand‑broadcasting the seed into raised beds 1. **Prep the bed surface** – Remove any standing dead plant material and smooth the soil with the wheel hoe so the surface is even. 2. **Mix the seed** – In a large bucket or tarp, combine the rye, vetch, clover (and radish if using) to keep the blend uniform. 3. **Divide the mix** – For 12‑15 raised beds (typical 4 × 8 ft) you’ll need about **4–5 lb of seed per bed**. Toss a handful into the center of each bed, then **walk around the perimeter** and sprinkle the rest as you go. 4. **Gentle incorporation** – Lightly rake the seed into the top ¼‑½ in (just enough to hide it from birds). You can also use the wheel hoe on a very shallow setting to drag the seed a little into the soil. 5. **Water** – Give each bed a **slow, deep soak** (≈ ½ in of water) right after seeding, then keep the soil consistently moist (≈ 1 in per week) for the first 7‑10 days. --- ### 5. Putting it all together – Timeline for central Ohio (Zone 5b/6a) | Week | Action | |------|--------| | **Early Oct** | Broadcast the rye/vetch/clover mix, water in, light‑rake. | | **Oct – Nov** | Keep soil moist; the cover will quickly fill the beds. | | **Late Jan – Early Feb** | If heavy snow cover is present, you can skip any extra watering. | | **Late Feb – Early Mar** (when shoots are 6‑8 in tall) | **Terminate** using one of the three hand‑tool methods above. | | **Mar (1‑2 weeks after termination)** | If you used “cut‑and‑bury,” lightly work the residue 2‑3 in deep; if you crimped, just let the mat sit. | | **Mid‑Mar** | Beds are ready for transplanting tomatoes, squash, and greens. | --- ### Quick‑check list for you right now - **Do you have a scythe or sickle?** If not, a cheap string‑trimmer (≈ $30 at Home Depot) set low works fine for the cut. - **Do you have a garden roller or a heavy board?** If not, a few brisk **step‑crimps** (walking over the dried rye) will do the job—just press down hard enough to flatten the stems. - **Do you want mulch left on the surface or a fully turned‑under “green manure”?** Pick the method (A vs. B) that matches your labor preference. Let me know which termination method feels most doable for you, or if you need suggestions for a particular tool you already own (e.g., converting the wheel hoe into a makeshift cutter). I can also walk you through the exact steps for a **cut‑and‑bury** using only a spade and hoe if that’s your preferred route. Happy fall planting!

Hold on — you said 12 to 15 beds, but that's not my setup. The whole plot is ¾ acre, but my actual growing surface is about 100 raised beds, mostly 4 by 10, and the rest is paths, my greenhouse, and a chicken coop. So I'm really seeding maybe a third of an acre of bed surface, not the full ¾. Does that 52 pounds of rye apply to the whole plot, or just the beds? I want to buy one 20-lb bag, not three and be stuck with leftover seed.

And just so you know — I do have a string trimmer, so cutting the rye in spring isn't a problem. I'm just not sure yet whether I'd rather crimp it and leave the mulch, or cut and bury it with my wheel hoe.

### 1. How much seed do you really need for **≈ 1/3 acre of beds**  

Your 100 beds at 4 × 10 ft each give you:

```
100 beds × 4 ft × 10 ft = 4 000 sq ft
```

But you said only about a **third of an acre** is actually planted (the rest is paths, greenhouse, coop).  

- **1 acre = 43 560 sq ft**  
- **⅓ acre ≈ 14 520 sq ft**  

Your 4 000 sq ft of beds is roughly **0.09 acre** (≈ 9 % of a full acre).  
If you want to seed **the whole planted area** (the 4 000 sq ft of beds) you can base the calculation on 0.09 acre, or you can spread the mix over the entire ⅓‑acre “cultivable area” (including any extra soil you might want to keep covered between beds). I’ll give numbers for both so you can pick the one that fits your layout.

| Target area | Acres | Rye needed | Vetch needed | Clover needed | Radish (optional) |
|-------------|-------|------------|--------------|---------------|-------------------|
| **Only the 100 beds (4 000 sq ft)** | 0.09 | **≈ 6 lb** (≈ 2.7 kg) | **≈ 0.9 lb** (≈ 0.4 kg) | **≈ 0.5 lb** (≈ 0.2 kg) | **≈ 0.2 lb** |
| **Whole cultivated ⅓ acre (≈ 14 520 sq ft)** | 0.33 | **≈ 23 lb** (≈ 10 kg) | **≈ 3.3 lb** (≈ 1.5 kg) | **≈ 1.7 lb** (≈ 0.8 kg) | **≈ 0.7 lb** |

**Take‑away:**  
- If you only want the **beds themselves** covered, **a single 20‑lb bag of winter rye is more than enough** (you’ll use about 6 lb). You’ll have ~14 lb left over, which you can either keep for next year or spread thinly over the pathways for extra winter mulch.  
- If you want to **cover the whole ⅓ acre** (including pathways) you’ll need roughly **23 lb of rye**. In that case you’d buy **one 20‑lb bag plus a small 5‑lb bag** (or a second 20‑lb bag if you prefer to have a buffer). The legume and clover portions are tiny – a 5‑lb bag of vetch and a 4‑lb bag of crimson clover will cover the whole area with plenty to spare.

**Recommended purchase list for the “bed‑only” approach (4 000 sq ft):**  

| Seed | Qty to buy (small‑bag size) | Approx. cost (2024) |
|------|----------------------------|---------------------|
| Winter rye (no‑hard‑seed) | 1 × 10‑lb bag (or 1 × 20‑lb bag, use 6 lb) | $12‑$15 |
| Hairy vetch | 1 × 2‑lb bag (you’ll use ~1 lb) | $5‑$7 |
| Crimson clover | 1 × 2‑lb bag (you’ll use ~0.5 lb) | $4‑$6 |
| Daikon radish (optional) | 1 × 1‑lb bag (you’ll use ~0.2 lb) | $2‑$3 |

That keeps the total seed purchase under **$30–$35** and leaves plenty of seed for a second season or for spot‑covering.

---

### 2. Termination Options with the **string trimmer** you already have

Both “crimp‑and‑leave” and “cut‑and‑bury” are doable; the choice hinges on how much **soil disturbance** you’re comfortable with and what you want the spring bed condition to be.

#### A. Crimp‑and‑Leave (Mulch)

1. **When to cut:** Late Feb – early Mar, when the rye is 6‑8 in tall and the vetch/clover have turned green but are not yet flowering heavily.  
2. **Cutting:** Run the string trimmer across the whole bed **in a single direction** (like mowing). A low‑cut head (½‑in) works best; you’re just trimming the tops, not shredding the whole stalk.  
3. **Crimping:**  
   - **DIY foot roller:** Take a 2‑ft‑diameter garden roller (or even a 5‑gallon bucket filled with sand) and push it over the cut stand **once or twice** while the stems are still a little flexible. The pressure flattens the stalks and breaks seed heads.  
   - **Step‑crimp alternative:** If you don’t have a roller, simply **walk firmly over the beds** (heel‑to‑toe) pressing down on the cut stalks. With a dense rye stand, a few firm steps flatten most of the blades.  
4. **Result:** A thick, brown “living mulch” that **suppresses weeds** and **releases nitrogen** as it decomposes. You can plant tomatoes, squash, or greens **directly into the mulch**—just make a small hole, backfill with the compost‑rich soil you already have, and set your transplant. No further tillage needed.

**Pros**  
- Minimal soil disturbance → preserves soil structure & microbes.  
- Saves a labor‑intensive “turn‑under” step.  
- Provides a protective mulch that moderates early‑spring temperature fluctuations.

**Cons**  
- If you want a *bare* seedbed for very delicate seedlings (e.g., lettuce), you may need to pull back a thin layer of the mulch or lightly rake it aside.  
- In a very wet spring the mulch can become a slick surface, making it a bit harder to walk.

#### B. Cut‑and‑Bury (Green Manure)

1. **When to cut:** Same timing (late Feb‑early Mar).  
2. **Cutting:** Use the trimmer to **trim the stand close to ground level** (≈ ½ in). You can make 2‑3 passes to ensure the stalks are short.  
3. **Burying with the wheel hoe:**  
   - Set the wheel hoe to its **shallowest setting** (≈ ½ in). Push the hoe **across the bed in a V‑shaped pattern**, which both cuts the remaining stubble and throws the material a few inches into the soil.  
   - After a complete pass, **flip the hoe** to a slightly deeper setting (≈ 1 in) and give the bed another pass, this time **mixing the chopped residue into the top 2‑3 in of soil**.  
4. **Water** the beds lightly and let the material decompose for **1‑2 weeks** before planting.

**Pros**  
- The incorporated biomass adds **organic matter directly into the root zone**, boosting soil tilth and water‑holding capacity.  
- Leaves a cleaner surface for transplanting delicate seedlings.

**Cons**  
- More physical work (two passes with the wheel hoe).  
- Slightly more disturbance of the soil structure you’ve built with your spader.

#### Which is easier for you?

- **If you like “set‑and‑forget”** and don’t mind a thin mulch layer when you plant, go with **crimp‑and‑leave**. It’s the fastest after the cut—just roll or step‑crimp once and you’re done.
- **If you want a truly clean seedbed** and are okay with a little extra hoe work, choose **cut‑and‑bury**. The extra organic matter will pay off in soil health and moisture retention.

---

### 3. Putting the numbers and the method together

| Scenario | Area seeded | Seed you’ll buy | What you’ll do in spring |
|----------|--------------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **Bed‑only (4 000 sq ft)** | 0.09 acre | 1 × 10‑lb rye (use 6 lb) + 2‑lb vetch + 2‑lb clover (+ optional radish) | Either **crimp‑and‑leave** (trimmer → foot roller) **or** **cut‑and‑bury** (trimmer → shallow wheel‑hoe passes). |
| **Full ⅓ acre (≈ 14 520 sq ft)** | 0.33 acre | 1 × 20‑lb rye + 1 × 5‑lb rye (or 2 × 20‑lb) + 5‑lb vetch + 4‑lb clover (radish optional) | Same two termination choices; the extra rye gives a thicker mulch if you crimp, or more organic matter if you bury. |

**Buying tip:**  
- Many seed companies (Johnny’s, High Mowing, Baker Creek) let you **order a custom “mix”** where you specify the exact pounds of each component. You can order a **15‑lb total mix** that contains ~10 lb rye, 3 lb vetch, 2 lb clover – perfect for your 4 000 sq ft.  
- If you prefer to buy a single bag, just grab a **20‑lb rye bag** and supplement with a **2‑lb vetch** and **2‑lb clover** bag; the extra rye can be saved for next year or used to thin‑cover the pathways.

---

### 4. Next step for you

1. **Confirm the exact area you want under cover** (just the beds or the whole ⅓ acre).  
2. **Pick a termination style** (crimp‑and‑leave vs. cut‑and‑bury). Let me know which feels more comfortable; I can give you a quick “step‑by‑step cheat sheet” for that method.  
3. I can also suggest a **specific seed‑order link** (e.g., Johnny’s 10‑lb rye + 2‑lb vetch + 2‑lb clover) if you’d like to place the order right now.

Give me a heads‑up on those two points, and I’ll fine‑tune the plan and the exact purchase list for you. Happy planting!

Okay wait, I've got to stop you for a second because that math made me do my own. 100 beds at 4 by 10… that's only 4,000 square feet, barely a tenth of an acre. I said a third of an acre earlier and I was just eyeballing the whole plot, not actually counting the beds. So I've been working from the wrong number this whole time.

That makes the seed thing way less scary, though — six pounds of rye instead of fifty-two? I can absolutely handle that, and one small bag of each covers it with room to spare.

But now that I realize the beds are actually small, I'm second-guessing the whole mix. In a 4-by-10 bed, is it really smart to cram in rye *and* vetch *and* clover all together, or should I keep it simple — rye over the whole thing, maybe throw clover in just a couple beds? I don't want a tangle I can't sort out with a trimmer come March.

### Small‑bed cover‑crop strategy – what works best in a 4 × 10 ft raised bed? When the planting surface is only **4 × 10 ft (40 sq ft)** you have two competing goals: 1. **Keep the soil covered all winter** – you need enough plant mass to form a living mulch. 2. **Make spring clean‑up doable with a string‑trimmer** – you don’t want a tangled jungle of vines that can’t be cut in a single pass. The good news is that **you don’t have to put every species in every bed**. You can treat the 100 beds as two simple “zones”: | Zone | What you sow | Why you do it | How much seed (per bed) | |------|--------------|---------------|--------------------------| | **A – “All‑grass” beds** (≈ 70 % of beds ≈ 70 beds) | **Winter rye only** (no‑hard‑seed, e.g., “Winter Rye – No‑Weed”) | - Fast to germinate, gives a thick straw‑like mulch that’s trivially cut with a trimmer.
- No climbing vines, so nothing to get tangled. | 0.05 lb (≈ 0.8 oz) of rye per 40 sq ft bed → **≈ 4 lb total** for 70 beds. | | **B – “Legume‑boost” beds** (≈ 30 % of beds ≈ 30 beds) | **Rye + a small legume blend** (hairy vetch + crimson clover) | - Adds nitrogen for the next spring’s heavy feeders (tomatoes, squash).
- The legume component is kept low‑density so it won’t overrun the rye and stays easy to cut. | **Rye:** 0.04 lb (≈ 0.6 oz) per bed → 1.2 lb total.
**Vetch:** 0.01 lb (≈ 0.15 oz) per bed → 0.3 lb total.
**Clover:** 0.005 lb (≈ 0.08 oz) per bed → 0.15 lb total. | **Result:** - **Total rye needed** ≈ **5 lb** (well under a 10‑lb bag). - **Total legume blend** ≈ **½ lb** (a single 2‑lb vetch bag and a 2‑lb clover bag give you plenty of spare seed). You can buy: - **1 × 10‑lb bag of winter rye** (you’ll use ~5 lb, the rest can be saved for next year or lightly broadcast on the pathways). - **1 × 2‑lb bag of hairy vetch** (you’ll use ~0.3 lb). - **1 × 2‑lb bag of crimson clover** (you’ll use ~0.15 lb). That’s the **simplest, cheapest, and least “tangled”** plan. --- ## Why the two‑zone approach works | Feature | All‑grass (rye‑only) | Mixed (rye + legume) | |---------|----------------------|----------------------| | **Winter ground cover** | Very dense straw mat – excellent weed suppression and mulch. | Still dense, because rye is the dominant component. | | **Nitrogen contribution** | Minimal (rye actually ties up a little N). | Vetch & clover fix ~10–15 lb N/acre‑equivalent, enough to boost the next tomato/squash crop in those beds. | | **Spring termination** | One trimmer pass, then either crimp (optional) or pull the straw aside. | Same trimmer pass; because the legume component is only ~10 % of the stand, the cut will still be clean and the stems stay flat enough to crimp or bury. | | **Risk of “night‑mare” vines** | None. | Very low – vetch climbs only on the rye blades and stops once the rye is cut low. | | **Labor** | Minimal – broadcast rye, water, let it grow. | Slightly more seed‑mixing, but still a single broadcast step. | --- ## Step‑by‑step for your 100 beds ### 1. Mix the seed (quick prep) 1. **All‑grass blend** – Put the 10‑lb rye bag in a large bucket, stir. 2. **Legume blend** – In a separate small bucket, combine the 2‑lb vetch and 2‑lb clover. Mix well. 3. **Combine for the mixed beds** – Take **½ cup** of the legume blend and mix it into **¾ cup of rye**. That ratio (≈ 10 % legume) is what you’ll broadcast on the 30 “B” beds. ### 2. Broadcast - **Rye‑only beds (70 beds):** Sprinkle the rye **evenly** across each 4 × 10 bed. A quick way is to **hold the bag open and let a 1‑inch stream fall** while you walk the bed lengthwise. Then lightly rake the surface to hide the seed. - **Mixed beds (30 beds):** Use the premixed rye + legume portion (the ½ cup + ¾ cup mixture) and broadcast the same way. ### 3. Water‑in - Give each bed a **slow, deep soak** (½ in of water). Keep the beds **moist for the first 7‑10 days** until seedlings are a few inches tall. After that, natural rain or occasional watering is fine. ### 4. Winter – let it grow - The rye will stay green through fall and turn brown in winter. The vetch & clover will flower early fall, then go dormant, but their roots keep nitrogen fixing. ### 5. Spring termination (your string trimmer is perfect) **Option 1 – Crimp‑and‑Leave (recommended for most beds)** 1. **Trim** the rye to about ½ in height with the trimmer. The legume stems will be cut at the same time. 2. **Crimp**: - If you have a **garden roller** (or a 5‑gal bucket filled with sand), push it over the beds **once** while the stems are still slightly flexible. - If you don’t have a roller, **walk firmly over each bed** (heel‑to‑toe) after trimming; the pressure flattens the stalks enough to stop seed set. 3. **Leave the flattened mat** on the surface. When you transplant, simply make a hole, backfill with a bit of compost, and set the seedling. The mulch protects the soil and releases N in the weeks after you plant. **Option 2 – Cut‑and‑Bury (if you prefer a clean bed)** 1. **Trim** the rye down to the soil surface with the trimmer (two passes if needed). 2. **Wheel‑hoe**: - Set the wheel hoe to its shallowest setting (≈ ½ in). Push it **across the bed in a V‑shaped pattern**; this cuts the remaining stubble and throws it a few inches into the soil. - Make a second, slightly deeper pass (≈ 1 in) to incorporate the cut material into the top 2‑3 in of soil. 3. **Water lightly** and let the green manure decompose for 1–2 weeks. Your beds will be ready for transplanting. ### 6. When to do it - **Ideal window:** **Late February to early March** in central Ohio (when the rye is 6‑8 in tall and the first hard freeze has passed). - **Weather tip:** Pick a dry weekend; a little rain after termination helps the mulch break down but too much rain can make the surface slick. --- ## Quick reference sheet you can print and stick in the shed | Bed type | Seed per 4 × 10 ft bed | How to broadcast | Spring termination | |----------|------------------------|-------------------|--------------------| | **Rye‑only** (≈ 70 beds) | 0.05 lb (≈ 0.8 oz) rye | Even sprinkle, light rake | Trim → crimp (roller or step) → leave as mulch | | **Rye + Legume** (≈ 30 beds) | 0.04 lb (≈ 0.6 oz) rye + 0.01 lb (≈ 0.15 oz) vetch + 0.005 lb (≈ 0.08 oz) clover | Same as rye‑only, using pre‑mixed blend | Same as rye‑only (the legume fraction is low enough to crimp cleanly) | --- ### Bottom line for you - **One 10‑lb bag of winter rye + a 2‑lb bag each of vetch and clover is more than enough** for all 100 beds. - **Keep the mix simple:** 70 % rye‑only, 30 % rye‑plus‑a‑tiny legume blend. - **Termination is easy** with the string trimmer you already own; either crimp‑and‑leave (least work) or cut‑and‑bury (cleaner bed) – both will keep the winter cover effective without creating a tangled mess.
